'''Sir John Bertram Adams''' {{postnominals|country=GBR|KBE|FRS}}<ref name="frs">{{Cite journal | last1 = Stafford | first1 = G. H. | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.1986.0001  | doi-access = free| title = John Bertram Adams. 24 May 1920 – 3 March 1984 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 32 | pages = 2–34| year = 1986 | jstor = 770106| s2cid = 72330820 }}</ref> (24 May 1920 – 3 March 1984)<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/03/08/obituaries/sir-john-bertram-adams-63-led-european-atomic-center.html |title=Obituary : Sir John Bertram Adams, 63; led European atomic center |access-date=2 September 2015 |work=The New York Times |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150524152535/http://www.nytimes.com/1984/03/08/obituaries/sir-john-bertram-adams-63-led-european-atomic-center.html |archive-date=24 May 2015 }}</ref> was an English [[accelerator physics|accelerator physicist]] and administrator.

Adams is mostly known for his work at [[CERN]] and [[Culham Centre for Fusion Energy|Culham Laboratory]]. Despite a lack of formal university education, Adams worked for organizations like the [[Telecommunications Research Establishment]] and the [[Atomic Energy Research Establishment]] in the 1940s and early 1950s. He served as acting director and eventually as elected director of [[CERN]], from 1976 until 1981.

== Biography ==

=== Early life ===
Born in [[Kingston, Surrey]] on 24 May 1920. He attended Eltham College from 1931 until 1936, after which he began to work for Siemens Laboratories in Woolwich. He continued studying at the South East London Technical Institute until 1939 earning a [[Higher National Certificate]]. Adams received no university education.<ref name="frs"/>

=== Professional career ===
At Siemens, his work was concerned with the acoustic properties of telephones. Between 1940 and 1945, he worked the [[Telecommunications Research Establishment]] being particularly responsible for developing the microwave radar<ref>{{Cite news|last=Waggoner|first=Walter H.|date=1984-03-08|title=SIR JOHN BERTRAM ADAMS, 63; LED EUROPEAN ATOMIC CENTER (Published 1984)|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/03/08/obituaries/sir-john-bertram-adams-63-led-european-atomic-center.html|access-date=2021-03-09|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> After, Adams moved to the [[Atomic Energy Research Establishment]] until 1953. In 1953, he moved once more to the new [[CERN]] Laboratory, serving in the General Physics Division as the engineer in charge of designing and building the [[Harwell Synchrocyclotron]], Europe's first large accelerator<ref name="frs" /> which operated successfully for 30 years until shutdown due to lack of funding. Also in late 1953, he was noted serving as a full staff member of the Proton Synchrotron Group. As CERN's proton synchrotron became fully operational in 1959, Adams was important to defining the methods and organization by which physicists would conduct testing. His work organizing CERN's administrative structure and measurement equipment were prepared for experimentation leading up until the synchrotron's start up at the end of 1959.<ref name="frs" /> After the death of [[Cornelis Bakker]], CERN Director-General, in April 1960, the Council of CERN appointed Adams to the post of acting Director-General.<ref>{{Cite web|title=J. B. Adams : acting Director-General|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1728417|access-date=1 September 2015|website=CERN Courier|date=1960 |publisher=CERN}}</ref>  He held this post until August 1961<ref>{{Cite web|title=Decisions of the 18th Council|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1728455|access-date=1 September 2015|website=CERN Courier|date=1960 |publisher=CERN}}</ref> when he returned to the UK as director of the [[Culham Fusion Laboratory]], and then from 1966 to 1971 he was a member of the [[United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority]]. He also became a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]]. Returning to CERN in 1971 as Director-General of Laboratory II, he led the design of the [[Super Proton Synchrotron]]. He split the duties of CERN Director General with [[Willibald Jentschke]] and then [[Léon Van Hove]] during the 1970s. His careful management of CERN's new projects were important to getting funding and approval from CERN's council. His designs were cautious and focused on reliability while providing the ability for new improvements to be built. The [[Super Proton Synchrotron]] was able to reach energies of 540 GeV.<ref name="frs" /> With the reorganization of CERN in 1976, he became the executive Director-General, working on obtaining funding for the [[Large Electron–Positron Collider|LEP collider]].<ref>{{cite journal|date=July 1984|title=Homage to Sir John|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1731044?ln=en|journal=CERN Courier|volume=24|issue=6|pages=232–236}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|date=April 1984|title=Sir John Adams 1920-1984|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1731006|journal=CERN Courier|volume=24|issue=3|page=91}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|date=December 1968|title=John Adams: Project Director|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1728926|journal=CERN Courier|volume=8|issue=12|page=310}}</ref> The new collider used magnet systems for acceleration that were designed by Adams in his previous accelerators.

He was chair of the International Committee for Future Accelerators, a working group of the [[International Union of Pure and Applied Physics]], from 1978 to 1982.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Membership {{!}} ICFA |url=https://icfa.hep.net/membership/ |access-date=2025-01-17 |language=en-US}}</ref>

Adams was knighted in 1981.

=== Personal life ===
Adams married Renie Warburton on 24 January 1943. They had two daughters and a son <ref name=":0" />. He resided in [[Founex]] ([[Vaud]]), Switzerland.<ref>''The Star Press'' (Indiana) 11 March 1984 page 38. Read on Newspapers.com on 26 March 2023.</ref>

== Awards and honors ==

* Rontegen Prize, University of Giessen (1960)
* D. Sc. (Honorary), University of Geneva
* [[Duddell Medal]], Physical Society (1961)
* D. Sc. (Honorary), University of Birmingham (1961)
* Fellow of Royal Society (1963)
* [[Leverhulme Medal (Royal Society)]] (1972)
* [[Royal Medal]], Royal Society (1977)
* [[Knight Bachelor]] (1981)

==John Adams Institute for Accelerator Science==<!-- redirect from [[John Adams Institute for Accelerator Science]] -->
The John Adams Institute for Accelerator Science (JAI), in the [[Denys Wilkinson Building#John Adams Institute for Accelerator Science|Denys Wilkinson Building]], an [[accelerator physics]] research institute comprising researchers from [[Royal Holloway, University of London]], [[University of Oxford]] and [[Imperial College London]] is named in his honour.<ref>{{cite web |title=History |url=https://www.adams-institute.ac.uk/about-john-adams-institute/history |website=John Adams Institute for Accelerator Science |access-date=1 February 2021 |archive-date=23 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210123043433/http://adams-institute.ac.uk/about-john-adams-institute/history |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=About us |url=https://www.imperial.ac.uk/john-adams-institute/about-us/ |website=John Adams Institute at Imperial College |access-date=1 February 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=John Adams Institute for Accelerator Science |url=https://www2.physics.ox.ac.uk/node/842 |website=University of Oxford Department of Physics |access-date=1 February 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=John Adams Institute for Accelerator Science |url=https://www.royalholloway.ac.uk/physics/research/particlephysics/johnadamsinstitute/johnadamsinstitute.aspx |website=Royal Holloway, University of London |access-date=1 February 2021}}</ref> A main road ("Route Adams") in CERN's Prevessin site is also named after him.
